interactions.summary: Students propose that Ulysses either flees purgatory or tries to seize godlike knowledge; Jiang accepts the purgatory-avoidance angle but rejects the stronger claim that this is the same as explicitly wanting to be God.

A student points out that Ulysses explicitly places wandering above father, son, and wife; Jiang answers that this is exactly the failure, because exploration without family love as an anchor becomes rootless ambition.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student observation with Jiang answer and follow-up question

claims.claim: Jiang accepts the idea that trying to bypass purgatory can paradoxically land one in hell.
Jiang rejects the simpler explanation that Ulysses is just trying to be God; he wants a more precise account of what is wrong with the voyage.
Jiang says Ulysses fails because he abandons the familial loves that should anchor exploration, leaving ambition as a wandering flame with no body to hold it.
The lecture's social anthropology here is that individuals are finally anchored by family, community, and society rather than existing as self-sufficient solitary beings.

signature_moments.moment: Ambition becomes a flame with no body: pure drive, no anchor.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's decisive image for why Ulysses' noble-seeming quest still belongs in hell.

signature_moments.moment: Trying to dodge purgatory may be the very move that delivers a soul to hell.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you try to run away from purgatory and you end up in hell
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses the class's best first answer to the Ulysses paradox.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's claim that exploration or selfhood only hold their shape when tethered to family and community rather than isolated ambition.
